urls.description: Every day, medicines improve health and save lives. But even medicines that have been carefully tested and assessed before they reach your medicine cabinet can sometimes cause side effects. Recognizing and reporting these side effects is essential to making medicines safer for everyone.From 2 to 8 November 2026, WHO joins the global #MedSafetyWeek campaign to raise awareness of the importance of recognizing side effects from medicines and encourage patients, caregivers and healthcare professionals to report them.Why reporting side effects mattersSide effects can take many forms, from a skin rash or upset stomach to changes in sleep, mood or other unexpected symptoms. Some may appear shortly after starting treatment, while others develop after prolonged use, a change in dose or when several medicines are taken together.Although medicines undergo rigorous evaluation before they reach patients, not all potential side effects can be identified during clinical trials. Continuous monitoring

note_tweet.text:
Nvidia reportedly asked TSMC to explore making 3D DRAM. 

"FAKE NEWS" was my knee-jerk reaction, but perhaps that's too strong.

Whatever's going on, it is NOT a near-term fix for the DRAM shortage.

TSMC is a logic chip maker, not a DRAM manufacturer - VERY different production requirements.

Patents show TSMC has explored 3D DRAM designs, but R&D and patents are a long way from mass production. 

TSMC can't simply convert a logic fab and start shipping. Equipment overlap helps, but developing the production process, qualifying the product and bringing it to mass production would be a multiyear undertaking.

Where does the specialized memory production technology come from? A licensing deal with a major memory maker? An acquisition? A JV? Otherwise, developing its own competitive 3D DRAM production process could take several years.

And even a licensing deal would not make production instant. Integration, qualification and yield still have to be solved.

The story's reference to TSMC's head of advanced packaging, Hsu Kuo-chin, is quite interesting. He used to be chairman of Micron Taiwan. He knows memory chips. Still, knowing and owning the IP are not the same.

My read: Nvidia wants 3D DRAM ready for a future product that needs higher bandwidth, lower power consumption, tighter integration with GPUs, etc. 

And that's a long term project.

note_tweet.text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?

TSMC WEIGHS MAKING 3D DRAM AT NVIDIA'S REQUEST

$TSM has reportedly begun drawing up plans to manufacture advanced 3D DRAM chips as AI-driven memory shortages push chip designers to seek additional supply, per The Information.

Unlike conventional DRAM, 3D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically to increase density.

The move could put TSMC in direct competition with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron.

No production timeline has been set. TSMC is considering building new fabs or converting an existing facility, but says its focus remains on its core logic foundry business.

note_tweet.text:
The Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) has once again lost all off-site power, forcing it to rely on emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential nuclear safety and security functions. 

The plant’s connection to its sole remaining external power line, Ferosplavna-1, was lost early this morning. It is the 27th such event during the conflict, underlining the continued precarious nuclear safety situation, IAEA @rafaelmgrossi says. 

The cause and location of the latest disconnection are not yet known. 

The IAEA team at the ZNPP has been informed that the plant currently has sufficient fuel reserves to operate a limited number of emergency diesel generators for around two weeks. 

DG Grossi stresses the importance of both restoring the ZNPP’s connection to the grid and increasing the amount of diesel fuel reserves available at the site.
